title: Improper Integral
body:
An [[Integral]] where the ordinary definition does not apply, because either the interval is
infinite or the integrand is. The [[Riemann Sum]] construction assumes a bounded function on a
bounded interval, so **an improper integral is not an integral until you define it as a
[[Limit]] of ones that are**:

$$
\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^t f(x)\,dx
$$

If that limit exists and is finite, the integral **converges** and equals it. Otherwise it
**diverges** and there is no answer to give. "Plug in infinity" is not a step; $\infty$ is not a
number and evaluating an antiderivative at it is shorthand for the limit, at best.

## The two kinds

**Type 1, infinite interval.** One limit at a time. For $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}$, split at any
convenient point and require **both halves to converge separately**. This matters: $\int_{-t}^{t}
x\,dx = 0$ for every $t$, but $\int_{-\infty}^\infty x\,dx$ diverges, because each half does. The
symmetric-limit value is called the principal value and it is not the same object.

**Type 2, infinite integrand.** The function has a vertical asymptote at an endpoint or, worse,
inside the interval. Approach the bad point with a limit:

$$
\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = \lim_{t\to 0^+}\int_t^1 \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x}} = \lim_{t\to 0^+}
\left(2 - 2\sqrt{t}\right) = 2
$$

**A discontinuity in the middle has to be found and split at.** Applying the
[[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] straight through $\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{dx}{x^2}$ gives $-2$, a
negative answer for a positive integrand, which is the standard way to lose the marks.

## The comparison everything is judged against

$$
\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^p}\ \text{converges} \iff p > 1
\qquad\qquad
\int_0^1 \frac{dx}{x^p}\ \text{converges} \iff p < 1
$$

Two thresholds, opposite directions, same exponent. **At infinity the function must decay faster
than $1/x$; at the singularity it must blow up slower.** $1/x$ itself fails both, which is the same
borderline the harmonic series sits on in [[Convergence Tests]], and not by coincidence: the
integral test is the statement that $\int_1^\infty f$ and $\sum f(n)$ converge together.

## Comparison test

Often you only need to know **whether** it converges, not what it equals, and the integral has no
elementary antiderivative anyway. If $0 \le f(x) \le g(x)$ on the interval:

- $\int g$ converges $\Rightarrow$ $\int f$ converges
- $\int f$ diverges $\Rightarrow$ $\int g$ diverges

Bounding above with something that converges, or below with something that diverges. The direction
that is useless is bounding above with something that diverges, which tells you nothing.
$\int_1^\infty e^{-x^2}dx$ converges because $e^{-x^2} \le e^{-x}$ for $x \ge 1$, and $e^{-x^2}$
has no elementary antiderivative to evaluate.

## Why it matters downstream

A [[Probability Density Function]] in [[STATISTICS]] is a non-negative function whose integral over
its whole domain is exactly $1$. For the exponential, normal, and gamma distributions that domain
is infinite, so **the density is only a legal density because an improper integral converges**.
Expectation and [[Variance]] are then improper integrals too, evaluated by
[[Integration By Parts]]. The Gaussian $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-x^2}dx = \sqrt{\pi}$ is the
famous case where the integral converges, has a beautiful closed form, and still cannot be got at
by antidifferentiation; it needs polar coordinates in two variables, which belongs to
[[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]].

## Related

- [[Integration Techniques]] for evaluating the proper integral inside the limit
- [[Convergence Tests]], and specifically the integral test, which is this idea for sums
- [[Limit]] in [[CALCULUS 1]], including limits at infinity, which is the machinery here
- [[Infinite Series]]: same question, discrete version. Both ask whether adding infinitely much of
  something smaller and smaller lands on a number
- [[Residue Theorem]] in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] evaluates the cases this note can only
  set up. Close the real line into a contour, show the arc contributes nothing, and read the answer
  off the enclosed poles; it works on integrals with no elementary antiderivative at all
